• Common name: Dwarf Water Lettuce
  • Scientific name: Pistia stratiotes
  • Difficulty: Easy
  • Lighting: Medium (grows fast under the right lighting)
  • pH: 6.0–7.5
  • Water hardness: Soft to medium
  • Temperature: 22–28 °C
  • Substrate: Not needed
  • Growth rate: Fast
  • Placement in tank: Floating
  • Height: small to very large; 5–25 cm
  • CO2: Not needed
  • Propagation: Sexual and asexual, via runners connected to daughter plants

Water lettuce is a herbaceous floating plant found all across the globe, especially in subtropical and tropical regions. It is found in marshes, bogs and lakes in every part of the world except Antarctica. It is also called Nile Cabbage or Water Cabbage because it looks like a leafy green vegetable.

It was reportedly introduced or discovered along the Nile River some 2000 years ago, and is mentioned in the writings of ancient Greek botanists and in ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics.
Dwarf Water Lettuce grows fast and takes up a lot of space; a single plant can cover a 75 cm tank in a fairly short time. The minimum recommended tank size is 40 litres; more is better.

Keep removing excess plants to prevent overcrowding and nutrient deficiency. Removing new daughter plants promotes further growth, while removing larger plants slows overall growth. Do not allow the plants to completely crowd the surface: pinch off plantlets or remove individuals to keep them spaced. This has to be done every week.

If the roots become too long (reaching the bottom or tangling in plants, decorations or the filter), pull the plants out every 2–3 weeks and cut the roots, leaving about 10 cm. The plant will survive.

In a small tank the plant may consume specific nutrients and turn yellow. Treat this with a natural nutrient booster or by adding a solution of the depleted nutrient.

Never submerge water lettuce. Its leaves have tiny hairs that repel water and let it float; if the leaves stay submerged for a long time they become wet and eventually die.

The plant does not need anything special to thrive. Optimal pH is 6.0–7.5. It thrives in warm water (22–30 °C) and only grows when the water temperature is above 18–20 °C. Low to moderate hardness (3–8 GH) is preferable; hard water (more than 12) stunts growth. It is extremely frost-sensitive and will not tolerate freezing temperatures.

Ideally it needs high humidity (70 or more), so partially close the aquarium with a lid.

Substrate: not needed. The plant floats and grows only on the water surface.

Lighting: medium light. A typical 10–12 hour cycle with full-spectrum lights is enough; small full-range T5 or T8 bulbs are sufficient. Introduce new plants to bright light or direct sunlight gradually, otherwise the leaves may scorch. Over-lit plants often turn reddish, yellow or brown and can grow too fast and too big.

Water flow: the less flow, the bigger the plant gets. To keep it small, use gentle flow. To stop the current pushing it around, use a barrier such as a floating rope or tube to confine it.

Supplements: no CO2 is needed. Fertilizer is not needed unless the water is very low in nitrates.

Water lettuce propagates both asexually and sexually. In home aquariums sexual propagation is uncommon. The flowers are tiny and sit in the centre of the plant, each plant bearing either a male or a female flower. After fertilization, berries with multiple seeds appear in the centre.

In aquariums asexual propagation is most common: small daughter plants float beside the mother plant, joined to it by a stolon. This forms thick mats, so take care that they do not completely cover the water surface. The plant grows quickly and puts out runners with daughter plants even when very tiny.

Dwarf Water Lettuce is a tropical perennial herbaceous plant that looks like a small, thick bush of cabbage-like leaves. The leaves are light green with parallel veins and wavy margins covered in short hair. The flowers are hidden in the middle of the leaves, and after fertilization the plant bears small, rounded berries. Underneath it has long white to blackish roots that may extend for more than 30 cm, providing breeding and hiding space.

Unlike standard Water Lettuce, which grows very big, the leaves of Dwarf Water Lettuce reach about 1.5–2.5 cm with no stem. However, if the water surface has no movement, the plant grows bigger over time, up to 10 cm or even more.

Benefits for the aquarium

  • Reduces algae: it out-competes algae for nutrients.
  • Reduces nitrates: it takes up nitrates and ammonia.
  • Natural filtration: it absorbs heavy metals, decaying food and fish, snail or shrimp waste.
  • Provides hiding places: the leaves and dangling roots give shade and shelter for fry, small or shy fish and shrimp.
  • Provides additional surface area for beneficial bacteria.

Tankmates

The dense roots shelter fish, shrimp and spawn, and the plant is compatible with most fish species. Avoid keeping it with goldfish or other herbivorous fish, which eat its roots. It is considered one of the best plants for a shrimp tank and can be kept with any shrimp species. Snails that do not harm it include ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, Japanese trapdoor snails and mystery snails. It is also a great choice for tanks with crayfish or crabs, which destroy and uproot other plants.

Common problems

  • Shedding roots: after shipping stress, the plant may shed its roots; they will grow back.
  • Fading: without enough light, the leaves become smaller.
  • Slow growth: water that is too hard or too cold, or not enough nutrients in the water column.
  • Yellowing: caused by strong light, ongoing nutrient deficiency or age. The oldest leaves at the bottom can simply be peeled off.
  • Mosquitoes: the dense hairs can serve as breeding ground for mosquito larvae.
  • Overgrowth: unchecked growth can shade out and kill plants below that need more light.
  • Submerged plants die and rot, ruining water quality.
  • Low humidity: dry, curling leaf ends are typically due to low humidity.

Quarantine

Always quarantine new plants before putting them into the tank. They can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs). They may also have been treated with pesticides, which are extremely poisonous to shrimp and invertebrates.

Buying

The plant is mostly sold in aquarium shops and garden centres. Plants received by mail may not look their best; let them recover for a short time in a small pot in a shaded area before moving them to the aquarium.
